Interpret a p-value alongside effect size and uncertainty. A p-value measures how unusual a test statistic is under the null model. Read it with the effect estimate and its uncertainty.
NHST is the common framework that tests data against a null hypothesis (H 0 ). A conventional cutoff is p ≤ 0.05 to reject H 0 .

The p-value is the probability of getting results as extreme as, or more extreme than, what we observed — assuming the null hypothesis is true . A probability for the null given the data requires a model for the alternative and prior odds between the hypotheses.
"Extreme" means far in the test statistic's null distribution. For z/t-based tests we standardize by the standard error. For other tests (e.g., χ², F), extremeness is on those statistics' own scales.

From Goodman's "A Dirty Dozen" — four mistakes that persist across research and industry: "If p = .05, the null has a 5% chance of being true." "A non-significant p (> .05) means no difference." "p = .05 means these exact data would occur only 5% of the time under H 0 ." "If you reject at p = .05, the Type I error probability for this decision is 5%." Power is the probability of rejecting the null for a specified effect size, design, and significance level. Set the effect size using the smallest difference that would change your decision.

Power analysis balances four interconnected parameters. Adjusting one changes the required sample size: α (Alpha) Type I error risk: probability of a false positive. Standard: 0.05 (5% risk). Lower α → larger sample needed. 1−β (Power) Probability of detecting a real effect when one exists. Standard: 0.80 or 0.90. Higher power → larger sample needed. δ (Raw Difference) Smallest effect of interest: the difference that would change your decision. Smaller difference to detect → much larger sample needed. σ (Standard Deviation) Noise level: natural data fluctuation. More noise → larger sample needed to separate signal.

For a two-sample t-test with equal group sizes, the central-t approximation provides a planning formula. Central-t approximation n = 2 × (t 1−α/2,df + t 1−β,df )² / d² where d = δ/σ (Cohen’s d), df = 2(n−1), and 1−β is target power. For a one-sided test use 1−α in place of 1−α/2. How the calculator finds n The calculator searches for the smallest whole n per group whose noncentral-t rejection probability meets the target. It uses both rejection tails for a two-sided alternative and the upper tail for a positive one-sided alternative. Since Cohen’s d = δ / σ , a smaller raw difference (δ) or a larger standard deviation (σ) both shrink d, which increases the required sample size. This is why noisy data and small effects are so expensive to study.
For the two-sample means example, the t reference accounts for estimating the common standard deviation. A normal-quantile calculation is an approximation for this setup.

The pooled-variance t-statistic follows a t-distribution under independent normal observations with a common variance. Welch’s procedure estimates separate variances and uses approximate degrees of freedom. The t-distribution is wider than the normal, especially for small samples. This means t-critical values are larger than Z-critical values , which means you need more observations to achieve the same power.

The t-distribution’s shape depends on degrees of freedom (df) . Define the unit, intervention, outcome, follow-up and target before choosing a comparison. In the synthetic example below, each unit can receive a one-time intervention at enrollment. The outcome is an event within 30 days. The target can be all eligible units or those who actually received treatment. Each unit has potential outcomes Y (1) under treatment and Y (0) under control. The average treatment effect (ATE) averages their difference across the eligible population. The average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) averages it over the population that received treatment. Identification asks whether the assumptions express that target using observable quantities. Estimation uses data to approximate those quantities. Proposed causal graph Target population Adjustment set Hidden cause contribution to outcome risk When does adjustment identify a total effect? A directed causal path points forward along every edge. A path such as T → C ← U → Y starts outward and can still carry a noncausal association after conditioning on C. A collider blocks a path until you condition on it or on one of its descendants. The back-door criterion is a sufficient adjustment rule. Choose a set with no descendants of treatment that blocks every path entering treatment through an incoming arrow. Use consistency between the specified intervention and observed outcomes, conditional exchangeability given the set, and treatment support for the target covariate values. Standardize the conditional arm means to the same target distribution. Conditioning on a mediator can remove part of the total effect and can introduce bias through shared causes of the mediator and outcome. A controlled direct effect requires a specified intervention on the mediator and additional identification assumptions. Specify the graph and estimand, identify the comparison, estimate it, then stress-test the assumptions. A placebo outcome or shuffled-label check can uncover a problem if the outcome or reference distribution respects the design. An unmeasured common cause can remain even after the check passes. Use matching or weighting when baseline adjustment is credible. Suppose hidden U affects treatment T and outcome Y, but its influence on the mediator M runs through treatment. At each measured baseline context X, M must intercept every directed T-to-Y path. X must block any back-door path from T to M, and T with X must block every back-door path from M to Y. Check support for each comparison. Mediator support in the synthetic data Treatment-to-outcome paths Compute the front-door contrast and examine one-sided support Within X, average each observed outcome mean at mediator value m over the observed treatment distribution. Then average these quantities using P(M = m | T = a , X) to get the interventional mean for arm a . Average those means across the eligible context distribution for the ATE. With known M(0) = 0 for every unit and the stated causal assumptions, the ATT can use the observed outcome mean among all treated units minus the mean of treated units with M = 0 in each context, weighted by the treated context distribution. Any treated context with no M = 0 comparison prevents this calculation. In symbols, this is the front-door formula: E[Y(a)] = Σ x P(x) Σ m P(m | a, x) Σ a′ P(a′ | x) E[Y | a′, m, x] . The ATE contrasts it at the two treatment values, and the ATT uses the treated-only calculation above. The offer example shows how restricting the offer group to openers changes the comparison.

Estimate treatment probabilities, check overlap, and build a comparison group by matching or weighting. Customers who join a loyalty program often spent more and ordered more frequently before joining. Matching and weighting use measured characteristics from before treatment to build a more comparable group, and balance diagnostics show how much of the measured differences remain. Unmeasured confounders can still bias the estimate.

A propensity score is the probability that a unit receives treatment given its observed covariates. Here, T indicates treatment and X represents the observed characteristics. e(X) = P(T = 1 | X) In observational studies, a model such as logistic regression or gradient-boosted trees estimates these probabilities. Matching pairs treated and comparison units with similar scores, stratification groups units into score ranges, weighting reweights units using their treatment probabilities, and regression adjustment includes the score as a covariate. A score of 0.7 means the model estimates a 70% chance that a unit with those characteristics receives treatment. Similar scores indicate similar estimated chances of treatment. Check overlap and balance on the measured covariates before relying on the comparison.

Common support means units in the target population have a meaningful chance of appearing in either the treated or comparison group. This simulated box plot illustrates what poor and good overlap can look like. Scroll the plot to see the full score range. With poor overlap, the matching caliper can leave treated units without a comparison, and weighting can give a few units very large weights. The matching tool below reports how many loyalty members had no non-member within the selected caliper.

Use characteristics measured before the index date, when the comparison starts. The program can change spending or ordering after that date, so matching on those later measures could remove part of the effect you want to estimate. In real data, members join on different dates. A control must have been eligible to join and still a non-member on the matched member’s index date. Use the same baseline and follow-up windows for both. Otherwise, a seasonal swing or a longer follow-up for one group can show up as a spending difference. Some controls will join later. Decide in advance whether to end their control follow-up when they join or keep them in the original group, and report that choice. If they stay in, the estimate compares joining on that date with not having joined yet, and some of the comparison group will be members by the end of follow-up. Choosing controls based on whether they eventually join uses information from after the index date. This simulated cohort has 3,000 customers. Every member joined in the same month. Every non-member was eligible and had not joined by then, and nobody joined during the six-month follow-up. The recorded characteristics are six-month average spend, spend in the last of those months, orders per month, months as a customer, and whether the customer is in the West region. Joining was more likely after an unusually high month of spending.

The dashed lines at ±0.1 are a common rule of thumb for flagging imbalance. They are not a statistical test. A characteristic inside the lines can still differ in spread, which the variance ratio column shows. Balance on measured characteristics says nothing about unmeasured ones. How balance is calculated Each standardized mean difference (SMD) divides the member-minus-non-member mean difference by the pooled standard deviation. The pooled standard deviation is the square root of the average of the two full groups’ sample variances. The same denominator is used before and after matching. Only the logit-score denominator changes with the baseline setting, because that setting refits the score model. The variance ratio divides the matched members’ variance by the matched non-members’ weighted variance. Both are mean squared deviations within the matched group. Ratios are shown for continuous measures only. ATT is the average effect of the program on all members. ATT M is the average effect on the members matched under the current settings, so it can change when the settings change who gets a match. The simulation knows both because it records each member’s spend with and without the program. In real data, only one of those is observed. How the matched estimates are calculated With membership denoted by T and receiving at least one control by M , ATT is E[Y(1) − Y(0) | T = 1] and ATT M is E[Y(1) − Y(0) | T = 1, M = 1]. For each matched member, subtract the average change among that member’s controls from the member’s change. Then average those differences, giving each matched member equal weight. ATT̂ M DiD = (1 / N M ) Σ i∈M [ΔY i − (1 / k i ) Σ j∈C i ΔY j ] N M is the number of matched members, C i is the set of controls for member i , and k i is the number in that set. ΔY is average monthly spend after the index date minus the selected baseline. For the matched post-join difference, use post-index spend in place of ΔY. The before-matching estimates are differences of simple means over all members and all non-members. Each time a non-member is chosen for member i , it receives weight 1/ k i . Add those shares across members to get that non-member’s total weight w j . The balance table uses these weights for the matched non-member means and variances. The effective sample size (ESS) of the controls is (Σw)² / Σw². A post-join comparison can still reflect differences in how much the groups would have spent without the program. DiD subtracts the baseline gap. If the matched groups would have changed by different amounts without the program, that difference in changes still enters the estimate. See parallel trends .

Distance. The propensity option matches on the log odds (logit) of the score estimated from baseline spend, orders, tenure and West region. Mahalanobis distance matches directly on those characteristics using their pooled within-group covariance. It works best with a few characteristics, because with many of them close matches become rare. Caliper. With either distance, a caliper rules out controls whose logit score differs from the member’s by more than the chosen number of pooled standard deviations. The pooled SD comes from all members and non-members before matching. A tighter caliper can change which controls are chosen and which members get a match. Compare the known ATT M across settings to see whether the target moved. The last column shows how far the estimate is from that target. Controls per member and replacement. Without replacement, each control is used once. Members matched later can get farther-away controls as the closest ones are taken. Reusing a close control can improve balance. When a few controls carry much of the weight, the effective sample size falls below the number of distinct controls. Taking three controls can improve precision, but the additional controls are at least as far away and may worsen balance. Baseline spend. This setting changes the spend measure used for matching and the baseline subtracted in DiD. Spending after an unusually high month tends to fall back toward the customer’s usual level. If members had the larger spike, using that month as the baseline can pull the estimate down. If controls had the larger spike, it can push the estimate up. In this cohort, the decision to join depended more on usual spending than on a single high month. Two customers can have similar spending in the last month even if it reflects a one-time purchase for one customer and typical spending for the other. Matching. With replacement, matched sets that share a control are dependent. For nearest-neighbor matching with replacement and a fixed number of controls per member, the ordinary bootstrap does not give valid standard errors in general. The Abadie–Imbens variance estimator accounts for reused controls. After matching without replacement, regression standard errors clustered on matched sets can be valid when there is overlap and the matches get closer as the sample grows, as shown by Abadie and Spiess. Weighting. Estimated propensities can improve precision in some designs. Standard errors that treat weights as fixed can be conservative or anticonservative. In a bootstrap, resample independent units or clusters and refit the full procedure. Explore pre-trend tests and sensitivity Earlier outcomes can reveal an implausible comparison. A true null can be rejected by chance, and noisy estimates can miss a consequential violation. With one pre-period there is no earlier change to test. Selecting a method or publication because a test passed can distort subsequent effect estimates and intervals. A fitted trend requires its own justification. This separate synthetic event study uses three leads, two post-period estimates and a common reference at event time −1. It assumes 80 independent assignment clusters and an asymptotic Gaussian distribution with the fixed covariance shown below. Use the drift control to ask how often a true linear violation would be detected. The sensitivity control applies to the same fixed estimates and targets the effect at event time 0. Drift in outcome units per period Pre-trend test Smoothness bound (outcome units per period²) At 0.50 outcome units of drift per period, the individual-lead screen detects the violation about 85% of the time. The 80% minimum detectable violation is 0.466 units per period. At smoothness bound M = 0.25, the robust 95% interval for the event-time 0 effect is 0.22 to 3.08 outcome units. The individual screen rejects if any single unadjusted 5% lead test rejects, so its overall false-positive rate can exceed 5%. The joint Wald test uses the full lead covariance and a 5% joint critical value. Detection probability and the 80% minimum detectable violation are specific to the proposed drift and test. This asks a different question from planning power to detect a treatment effect . The smoothness restriction bounds changes in the slope of the underlying untreated-gap path, including the first post-period. A relative-magnitude restriction instead bounds post-period first differences by a multiple of the largest absolute underlying pre-period first difference. Sampled leads have uncertainty. Use a common reference and carry the full covariance, including when converting adjacent contrasts. The identified range below plugs in the pre-period path and omits sampling error. The HonestDiD fixed-length confidence interval (FLCI) uses a fixed half-width to account for sampling uncertainty and the largest bias allowed by the selected restriction. It was computed with the HonestDiD R package, version 0.2.8. Pre-trend sensitivity Panel-based counterfactual methods Synthetic control, synthetic DiD and TROP use repeated outcomes from untreated comparison units to estimate what would have happened to the treated units without the intervention. It assumes that the weighted blend of comparison units that reproduces the treated unit’s pre-treatment outcomes would have continued to track its untreated outcomes after treatment. t: A service awards a fee waiver when an application score reaches 50. The running variable is the score, and the first eligible score is 50. Continuity means that, absent the change in eligibility, each relevant potential-outcome mean would change smoothly through 50. With deterministic receipt, eligibility and receipt jump together. Adjust a spending model when customer outcomes are selectively observed. Estimate a spending equation when linked spending is observed for only part of the customer population.

Every customer has monthly spending during the measurement window, but spending is recorded only for customers who link their receipts. In this example, 1,206 of 2,000 customers link. Customers earn reward points in proportion to what they spend, so customers who spend more have more reason to link. Longer-tenured customers spend more on average, but even among customers with the same tenure, those who spent more than usual are more likely to link. As a result, linked customers spend more on average than unlinked customers with the same tenure. A regression fitted only to linked customers inherits this difference. In this example, it overstates spending at every tenure, and most at short tenures, where fewer customers link and the ones who do are furthest above average. It therefore also understates how much spending rises with tenure. Averaged over all 2,000 customers’ tenures, its predictions come to $113.36 a month. The true spending equation gives $103.70. Linking that depends only on tenure would not cause this. Linked and unlinked customers with the same tenure would then spend the same on average, so a regression on linked customers would still estimate the population relationship, as long as it has the right form. In this example spending rises in a straight line with tenure, so a straight-line regression has the right form. The bias comes from linking that depends on the part of spending tenure doesn’t explain. Heckman’s correction models who links alongside spending and uses that model to adjust the spending regression. The worked example below follows the two-step correction from the selection equation to the corrected spending regression and explains what each part assumes. The result describes spending for all customers. It does not measure whether linking receipts changes spending, which would need a treatment comparison.
STEP 1 Probit on all customers → EXTRACT Mills Ratio (λ) → STEP 2 Observed spending on X and λ → RESULT Corrected spending equation

For each of the 2,000 simulated customers, we know their tenure in months, whether they received a reminder, and whether they linked their receipts. Set the reminder indicator to 1 for customers who received it and 0 otherwise. Set S = 1 when the customer linked and S = 0 otherwise. Spending is observed for the 1,206 customers who linked, or 60.3% of the sample. Fit a probit on all customers. The coefficients γ 0 , γ 1 , and γ 2 are the intercept, tenure coefficient, and reminder coefficient in the linking model. The linear index Zγ adds the intercept to the tenure and reminder terms. The standard normal cumulative distribution Φ converts that index to a linking probability. P(S = 1 | tenure, reminder) = Φ(γ 0 + γ 1 × tenure + γ 2 × reminder) The reminder was randomly assigned with a 50% probability and sent after the spending window closed. It changes whether customers link existing receipts, and spending for the window is already fixed. This is the exclusion restriction. If the reminder also changed spending, the correction would mix that change with selection. With the reminder in the probit, the inverse Mills ratio can vary between customers with the same tenure. With tenure alone, the method relies on the curvature of the ratio to estimate separate coefficients for tenure and the ratio. The result section shows how much precision that costs. If some customer profiles have very little chance of linking, their spending predictions rely more heavily on extrapolation.

For each linked customer, calculate the inverse Mills ratio λ from the fitted linking index Zγ̂. The hat marks an estimate, and φ is the standard normal density. λ̂ = φ(Zγ̂) / Φ(Zγ̂) This calculation uses the coefficients from Step 1. If the unexplained parts of linking and spending are jointly normal given the predictors, the average spending error among linked customers with index Zγ is ρσλ. Here ρ is the correlation between the two errors and σ is the standard deviation of the spending error. The simulation draws the errors this way, with ρ = 0.60 and σ = $30. In real data, joint normality is an assumption. If it fails, the ratio generally gives the wrong correction for the average spending error. The linked customer with a 17.77% estimated linking probability has a ratio of 1.465. At 93.97%, the ratio falls to 0.127. With a positive error correlation, higher linking probabilities mean less upward bias in the average spending of customers who link.

Regress spending on tenure and the fitted ratio using the linked customers. In the diagram, X contains the intercept and tenure. In this equation, β 0 is the intercept, β 1 is the change in average spending per month of tenure, and β λ is the coefficient on λ̂. That last coefficient estimates ρσ, which equals $18 in the simulation. spending = β 0 + β 1 × tenure + β λ × λ̂ + error Ordinary least squares (OLS) assumes equal error variance across linked customers for its usual standard errors. Here the variance changes with the ratio. The usual standard errors also treat the ratio as fixed, even though its estimated inputs carry sampling error from Step 1. The two-step standard errors account for both. Here they are larger for all three coefficients. The standard error for the ratio coefficient rises from $3.027 to $3.143. Under the model’s assumptions, testing β λ = 0 tests whether linking depends on the unexplained part of spending. Failure to reject can reflect low precision, so selection bias can still be present.

OLS on linked customers estimates a tenure slope of $0.78 per month. The Heckman fit with the reminder puts it at $1.01, close to the true $1.00. The average predicted spending in the table uses each row’s intercept and tenure slope at all 2,000 customers’ tenure values. It is $113.36 for OLS and $103.29 for the corrected equation, compared with $103.70 from the true spending equation. The customers’ simulated spending averages $103.16. The gap is the average of their random spending errors. The corrected line uses the estimated intercept and tenure slope from Step 2, β̂ 0 + β̂ 1 × tenure. The dashed curve describes expected spending among linked customers. It adds the fitted ratio coefficient times the average ratio for linked customers at each tenure. To compute that average, weight each reminder group by its assignment probability times its fitted linking probability at that tenure. Inspect plotted spending values Inspect individual customer points The OLS line approximates the dashed curve, with a largest gap of $1.01 across the plotted tenure values. The light grey points show the unlinked customers’ spending, which is visible only in the simulation. Interpret spending here as net of refunds, so it can be negative. Without the reminder, the fitted ratio is nearly a straight-line function of tenure among linked customers. Their correlation is −0.997 without the reminder and −0.574 with it. The second step can barely separate the two terms. Without the reminder, the intercept is $84.51, the tenure slope is $0.939 per month, and the ratio coefficient is $10.21. The intercept’s standard error rises from $3.33 to $49.43 and the slope’s rises from $0.073 to $0.753. The spending equation assumes a straight-line relationship with tenure. If that relationship is curved, a straight line can miss the population average at some tenures even after correcting for selection. The corrected equation describes average monthly spending at each tenure across all customers, including those who never linked their receipts. Key Definition Uplift is the difference between conversion probabilities under treatment and control for a baseline profile. Only one outcome is observed for each customer.

Two ways to estimate conversion lift by baseline profile are shown below. T-Learner: Train separate models for treatment and control, then subtract predictions. Class Transformation: Combine assignment and the observed outcome into a target whose conditional expectation can estimate uplift under the known randomization probabilities.

Score a profile using its predicted conversion rates under the two assignments. A model can estimate the average lift for a profile, even when its individual response types are unknown. Sleeping Dogs Would convert under control and would not convert under treatment. h: Which arrows can the data orient?
t: The Path Workbench fits the graph you draw. Here, use conditional independence to learn which arrows the three-node PC exercise can orient. The synthetic examples are jointly Gaussian, where zero partial correlation corresponds to conditional independence. Graph that generated the evidence Start with all three possible edges. Look for evidence to remove A—C. Then ask whether B belongs to the set that separated them. When is the equivalence class justified? PC assumes an acyclic data-generating graph, causal sufficiency (no unmeasured common causes among the modeled variables), the causal Markov and faithfulness conditions, and suitable independence tests. Exact cancellation between paths can create a population independence that violates faithfulness. Sampling noise can also make a real association hard to detect, even under faithfulness. Under the assumptions, the population target is a completed partially directed acyclic graph (CPDAG). A CPDAG summarizes graphs with the same conditional-independence implications. An undirected edge can have either direction across members of the equivalence class, with directions sometimes changing together. An intervention can supply directional evidence. A null response alone can reflect poor measurement, low power, cancellation, or an absent effect. Return to the Path Workbench to fit a specified graph, or to Causal Graphs and Identification to assess identification for an assumed graph.

Understand the churn analysis pipeline — click any step to learn more.

Aggregate activity metrics: login frequency, support tickets, feature usage, session duration. Churn models need behavioral signals, not just demographics. The most predictive features tend to be changes in behavior — a customer who logged in daily and now logs in weekly is a stronger signal than a customer who always logged in weekly. Collect: login timestamps, feature usage events, support tickets (volume and sentiment), billing events, NPS/CSAT responses, and session duration trends. Store as time-series so you can compute rolling averages and deltas.

Estimate each customer’s churn probability from behavioral signals. Gradient-boosted trees such as XGBoost or LightGBM can handle mixed feature types, missing data, and non-linear relationships. Compare them on held-out data with a simpler baseline such as logistic regression. The model outputs a probability (0–1) for each customer. Key signals typically include: declining activity velocity , increasing support ticket frequency, reduced feature breadth, and payment failures. Train on historical churn labels with a rolling window approach to avoid data leakage.

Group customers into risk tiers (Low, Medium, High) based on probability thresholds. Don’t just use arbitrary thresholds (e.g., > 0.7 = high risk). Instead, calibrate thresholds based on your intervention capacity . If your team can handle 50 save-calls per week, set thresholds so the “high risk” segment is roughly that size. Use precision-recall curves to find the threshold that maximizes caught churners while keeping false positives manageable. Revisit thresholds monthly as your model and customer base evolve.

Test which interventions change retention before targeting by risk. A churn risk score estimates who is likely to leave. The score alone cannot tell you whose retention an offer would change. Some high-risk customers leave even with an offer, and contact can prompt others to leave sooner. Candidate interventions range from personal outreach, discounts, and contract flexibility to lower-cost automated emails and feature education. Randomize the offer within each risk tier and compare retention with a holdout group in the same tier. Use the measured change in retention to choose whom to contact. h: Describe a market with segment shares
t: A segment’s share is the fraction of an area’s households that belong to it. The household count is how many households that is. Report both when you compare a candidate site with an existing store’s trade area. A larger area can have the same share and many more households in the segment. A segment assigned by postal code describes the area as a whole, and the households in it vary. To estimate spending or profitability for individual customers, match your own customer records to segments at the household level. Before using a segment’s share to choose a site, check whether your existing stores with a higher share of that segment have higher sales.
Measure which products appear in the same basket or in a later purchase. Measure how often products appear together in a basket or in later purchases by the same customers.
These four ratios use baskets as the unit of analysis. Count each product at most once per basket.

Support = (Baskets containing X & Y) ÷ (Total baskets) Support tells you how common the pair is. A high-support pair shows up in many transactions. But support alone can be misleading—two popular items will naturally co-occur often, even with no real affinity. Support Support(X → Y) = P(X ∩ Y) = count(X and Y) / count(all baskets)

Attached Rate = (Baskets containing X & Y) ÷ (Baskets containing X) Given someone bought X, what fraction also bought Y? This is the conditional probability P(Y|X). A 40% attached rate means Y also appears in four of every ten baskets containing X. Attached rate (confidence) Confidence(X → Y) = P(Y | X) = count(X and Y) / count(X)

Affinity = Attached Rate ÷ P(Y) Affinity divides the observed attached rate by the overall rate for Y. Values above or below 1 indicate more or less co-occurrence than expected if the items were independent. Affinity (lift) Lift(X → Y) = P(Y | X) / P(Y) = Support(X,Y) / [P(X) × P(Y)]

Cherry pick rate = (Baskets containing Y but not X) ÷ (Baskets containing Y) This is the share of baskets with Y that omit X. Even one purchase of Y without X gives a 100% rate if that is the only purchase of Y. Read it alongside the purchase count. Cherry pick rate Cherry Pick(Y given X) = count(Y without X) / count(Y) = 1 − P(X | Y)

Imagine 100 baskets. Product X appears in 40 baskets. Product Y appears in 30 baskets. Both X and Y appear together in 20 baskets. Metric Calculation Result Support 20 / 100 0.20 (20%) Attached Rate 20 / 40 0.50 (50%) P(Y) 30 / 100 0.30 (30%) Affinity (lift) 0.50 / 0.30 1.67× Cherry Pick (30 − 20) / 30 0.33 (33%) Interpretation An affinity of 1.67 means baskets containing X are 67% more likely to contain Y than baskets overall. The attached rate of 50% means half of the baskets containing X also contain Y. The cherry pick rate of 33% means a third of the baskets containing Y exclude X.

For a customer at origin i , the Huff model divides store j ’s attractiveness adjusted for distance by the sum across eligible stores. P ij = (A j α / D ij β ) ÷ Σ k (A k α / D ik β ) In this example, A is store size and D is distance. The exponent α controls the importance of size. A larger positive β discounts distant stores more sharply. Review Reading Regressions for help interpreting the coefficients.

This example trains on trips with exactly two available stores. Provide one row per trip in paired_store_choices with chosen_a (0 or 1), size_a , size_b , distance_a_km , and distance_b_km . The log odds of choosing A over B are the differences in their log utilities. The fitted size coefficient is α and the negative of the distance coefficient is β. CREATE OR REPLACE MODEL `project.dataset.huff_model` OPTIONS ( MODEL_TYPE = 'LOGISTIC_REG', INPUT_LABEL_COLS = ['chosen_a'], FIT_INTERCEPT = FALSE, DATA_SPLIT_METHOD = 'NO_SPLIT' ) AS SELECT chosen_a, LN(size_a) - LN(size_b) AS log_size_ratio, LN(GREATEST(distance_a_km, 0.1)) - LN(GREATEST(distance_b_km, 0.1)) AS log_distance_ratio FROM `project.dataset.paired_store_choices` WHERE chosen_a IN (0, 1) AND size_a > 0 AND size_b > 0 AND distance_a_km >= 0 AND distance_b_km >= 0;

h: Predict shares with the fitted weights
t: The prediction query expects one row per eligible origin–store pair in store_choice_inputs , with origin_id , store_id , square_footage , distance_km , and spend_potential . Use the same distance measure and units in both queries. Straight-line distance and driving time measure different things and call for separate fits. The 0.1 km floor keeps coincident points finite. WITH coefficients AS ( SELECT MAX(IF(processed_input = 'log_size_ratio', weight, NULL)) AS alpha, -MAX(IF(processed_input = 'log_distance_ratio', weight, NULL)) AS beta FROM ML.WEIGHTS(MODEL `project.dataset.huff_model`, STRUCT(FALSE AS standardize)) ), scores AS ( SELECT origin_id, store_id, spend_potential, alpha * LN(square_footage) - beta * LN(GREATEST(distance_km, 0.1)) AS log_utility FROM `project.dataset.store_choice_inputs` CROSS JOIN coefficients WHERE square_footage > 0 AND distance_km >= 0 ), utilities AS ( SELECT *, EXP(log_utility - MAX(log_utility) OVER (PARTITION BY origin_id)) AS utility FROM scores ), shares AS ( SELECT origin_id, store_id, spend_potential, SAFE_DIVIDE(utility, SUM(utility) OVER (PARTITION BY origin_id)) AS choice_probability FROM utilities ) SELECT origin_id, store_id, choice_probability, spend_potential * choice_probability AS expected_spend FROM shares; Validate the coefficients and predicted shares on held-out trips. Applying a two-store fit to larger choice sets assumes the same utilities and that relative odds for two stores stay stable when alternatives are added. Expected spend also assumes the input spend is allocated among the listed stores.

Choose a comparison to estimate what enrollment changed. Estimate how spending would have changed for members had they stayed out of the loyalty program.

h: Why member spending is a poor baseline
t: Customers who already buy frequently may be more likely to join. If they would have spent more anyway, a post-enrollment comparison overstates lift. If members would have spent less than nonmembers without the program, the post-enrollment comparison understates lift. The direction of bias depends on who joins and how their spending would have changed without the program. To see this as a causal graph, open Causal Graphs and Identification and choose Unmeasured common cause . Its hidden U plays the role of a trait such as engagement that affects both joining and spending.

If you can randomize who receives an invitation, compare outcomes by invitation assignment. That estimates the effect of the invitation, including customers who decline. Encouragement and uptake shows how to estimate the effect of joining among customers who join only when invited, and the assumptions that estimate requires. If you have historical enrollment data, compare pre- and post-enrollment spending with a credible untreated group and check baseline overlap, pre-program trends, and concurrent changes. Match the cohort builds that group for a simulated loyalty cohort whose members spent more before joining. The Difference-in-Differences Lift Calculator then compares spending changes for those members and their matched controls. To evaluate profitability, compare incremental contribution margin over the same follow-up window with rewards, discounts, and operating costs.

Each cell shows the t-critical value for the given degrees of freedom (df) and significance level (α). The α = 0.05 two-tailed column is highlighted as the most commonly used threshold. Scroll the table to see more columns on narrow screens. Reading the Values All values are positive . For a two-tailed test, the critical region is |t| > t-critical (both tails). For a one-tailed test, use the one-tailed α row and apply the cutoff in the prespecified direction. Values are computed from the inverse t-distribution.

Find your degrees of freedom (df) in the leftmost column. For a pooled-variance two-sample t-test: df = n 1 + n 2 − 2. Welch’s test uses Welch–Satterthwaite degrees of freedom. The lookup rounds fractional df down to use a conservative critical value. For a one-sample test: df = n − 1. For regression coefficients: df = n − k − 1 (where k is the number of predictors). Choose your significance level (α) across the top. The standard in most fields is α = 0.05 (two-tailed), which corresponds to a 95% confidence level. Read the intersection. The value at (df, α) is the critical t-value. For a two-sided test, reject if |t| exceeds this value. For a prespecified upper-tail test, reject if t exceeds it. For a lower-tail test, reject if t is below its negative.

The table shows two rows of alpha values in the header: Two-tailed α: Used when your alternative hypothesis is “μ ≠ μ 0 ” (the effect could go either direction). The critical region is split across both tails. This is the default in most research. One-tailed α/2: Used when your alternative hypothesis specifies a direction (“μ > μ 0 ” or “μ < μ 0 ”). The entire rejection region is in one tail. A two-tailed α = 0.05 corresponds to a one-tailed α = 0.025. If you are running a one-tailed test at α = 0.05 , look at the column where the one-tailed row says 0.05—which is the two-tailed α = 0.10 column.

As degrees of freedom increase, the t-distribution converges toward the standard normal (Z) distribution. The last row of the table (∞) shows the Z-critical values. For df ≥ 120, the difference between t and Z is negligible. Significance level (α): Scroll the table to see more columns on narrow screens. How to Use Your F-statistic comes from an ANOVA or regression output. Compare it to the critical value at the intersection of your df 1 (numerator degrees of freedom) and df 2 (denominator degrees of freedom). If F obs > F crit , the result is statistically significant at the chosen α.

Unlike the t-distribution (which has one df), the F-distribution has two degrees-of-freedom parameters: df 1 (numerator): In one-way ANOVA, this is k − 1 , where k is the number of groups. In regression, it is the number of predictors. df 2 (denominator): In one-way ANOVA, this is N − k , where N is the total number of observations. In regression, it is N − p − 1 .

h: What the F-test is used for
t: ANOVA (Analysis of Variance): Tests whether the means of two or more groups are all equal. The F-statistic compares between-group variance to within-group variance. Overall regression significance: Tests whether at least one predictor in a regression model has a non-zero coefficient. This is the F-statistic reported at the bottom of regression output. Comparing variances: For two independent normal samples, the ratio of their sample variances follows an F-distribution under equal population variances. A two-sided alternative rejects unusually small or unusually large ratios.

F and t Connection F = t² (when df 1 = 1) When comparing exactly two groups , a one-way ANOVA with df 1 = 1 gives the same p-value as the two-sided pooled-variance t-test. The F-statistic is the square of the t-statistic, and the p-values are the same. This means an F-table with df 1 = 1 gives you the square of the corresponding t-critical value. Relation to the t-distribution Like the t-distribution , the F-distribution has a CDF that can be written using the regularized incomplete beta function. If you are doing a simple two-group comparison, you can use either table—t is more natural for directional hypotheses, F for omnibus tests. See our Sample Size & Power page for how these distributions feed into study design.

Assigning credit for conversions or revenue to channels or touchpoints. Rules such as first-touch and last-touch, Markov removal effects and survey responses describe how credit is divided. Estimating how many conversions a channel added requires a causal comparison such as a holdout.

The average of Y(1) − Y(0), the difference between a unit’s potential outcomes with and without treatment. The ATE averages over the eligible population, the ATT over the units that received treatment, and the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) over units with a specified baseline profile.

How similar treated and comparison groups are on measured baseline characteristics, often summarized by standardized mean differences (SMDs). After randomization, balance checks help diagnose implementation. After matching or weighting, they show how much measured difference remains. They say nothing about unmeasured characteristics.

Has three meanings in the guide. In experiments and comparisons, a baseline is a measurement or characteristic recorded before treatment, such as prior spend. In a marketing mix model, baseline is the modeled demand under the model’s reference inputs, outside the media terms. In Markov attribution, the baseline probability is the chance of conversion with every channel present.

Randomizing separately within groups of similar units, such as baseline activity bands, so each block is split between arms in the planned proportions. When allocation fractions differ across blocks, weight each within-block difference by the block’s share of enrollment.

The smallest effect at which an action covers its cost. It is a business threshold, separate from statistical significance: an estimate can differ from zero and still fall short of break-even. With contribution margin m and media as the only incremental cost, the break-even incremental revenue ROAS is 1/m.

Adjusting one estimate with evidence from another source. Holdout calibration rescales platform-reported credit by the ratio of a past holdout’s incremental conversions to the conversions the platform reported during the test. Calibrating a marketing mix model uses a lift test as a prior or likelihood for a channel’s effect. Both assume the test evidence transfers to what is being adjusted. Survey calibration compares survey-implied ROAS with platform-reported ROAS.

The part of an ad’s effect that continues after the week it runs. In an adstock transformation, the carryover rate λ is the fraction of exposure retained each week, and the half-life is the time for the remaining exposure from one spend pulse to fall by half.

Churn is the share of customers who leave over a period, and retention is the share who stay. Compare cohorts at the same time since signup, with a common definition of churn and a known end date for the data. A churn risk score predicts who is likely to leave. It does not show whose retention an offer would change.

A group defined by a shared starting event and followed over time. The guide uses signup cohorts for retention, adoption cohorts that start treatment on the same date in difference-in-differences, daily assignment cohorts in an A/B test, and a matched cohort of members and controls.

A range from a procedure that, under its assumptions, covers the true value at a stated rate, such as 95%, in repeated samples. Its half-width, the margin of error, is a critical value times the standard error. A Bayesian credible interval instead assigns probability to the parameter given the priors and data. In market basket analysis, “confidence” means the attached rate, not an interval.

A common cause of treatment and outcome that mixes the treatment effect with preexisting differences in a raw comparison. Random assignment breaks the link between treatment and confounders. Observational designs adjust for measured confounders and remain open to bias from unmeasured ones.

Units that do not receive the treatment, used to estimate what the treated units’ outcomes would have been without it. Random assignment makes the control group comparable by design. An observational comparison group, including matched controls, is comparable only under assumptions such as exchangeability or parallel trends.

Spend divided by conversions. The Budget Decision Engine compares current CPA with a goal. A cost per incremental conversion instead divides spend by the conversions a test estimates the spending added.

h: Critical value and degrees of freedom
t: A critical value is the cutoff a test statistic must exceed to reject the null hypothesis at a chosen significance level. For t and F tests it depends on the degrees of freedom, which grow with sample size. As degrees of freedom grow, the t-distribution approaches the normal.

The value a customer generates over the relationship. The guide estimates it from historical averages, or for subscriptions by discounting expected monthly gross profit under a churn probability. Under a contract, churn is observed. Without one, whether a customer is still active has to be inferred, as in BG/NBD.

Treated and comparison groups would have the same average outcomes under the same treatment. Random assignment makes groups exchangeable by design. Conditional exchangeability requires this only within levels of measured covariates, which means no unmeasured confounding given those covariates.

An experiment that assigns a spend change to markets rather than to individuals. In a paired geo test, markets are matched in pairs, one market in each pair is randomly assigned the change, and the effect is estimated from the paired differences. Markets must not affect each other’s outcomes.

A randomly selected group withheld from a campaign or treatment and used as the control. Comparing it with the exposed group estimates incremental outcomes. Holdout results can also calibrate platform-reported credit and marketing mix models.

The change in an outcome caused by a campaign or treatment: outcomes with it minus the outcomes that would have occurred without it. Observed or attributed revenue includes sales that would have happened anyway, so estimating incrementality requires a causal comparison such as a randomized holdout.

The effect of assignment, comparing outcomes by assigned group whether or not units took up the treatment. Random assignment identifies it, given complete follow-up and no interference. The effect of actual receipt among compliers, a local average treatment effect (LATE), also requires relevance, no direct effect of assignment, and monotonicity.

A measured quantity that tracks a business outcome, with a defined unit, denominator and follow-up window. A measurement plan connects each KPI to the events that record it. In a marketing mix model, the KPI is the outcome the model fits, such as revenue.

In an experiment, the difference in an outcome between treatment and control, such as conversion-rate points. Relative lift divides that difference by the control rate. A lift test is an experiment that measures it. In market basket analysis, lift (affinity) divides the attached rate for a pair by the overall rate for the second item. A value of 1 means the items appear together as often as expected if they were independent.

A model of aggregate sales or another KPI as baseline demand plus modeled media response and other measured drivers such as prices and promotions. Different channel contributions can fit the same sales history. Interpreting a modeled response as the effect of a spend change requires a credible causal comparison, such as a lift test.

A variable on the path from treatment to outcome, such as search interest between advertising and sales. The total effect combines the direct path and the indirect path through the mediator. Adjusting for a mediator removes part of the total effect.
The smallest true effect a design would detect with the target power at the chosen significance level. It describes sensitivity against zero, which is different from clearing a break-even threshold.

Testing several arms, outcomes or subgroups raises the chance that at least one shows a false positive. Bonferroni and Holm corrections control the family-wise error rate. Benjamini–Hochberg controls the expected false-discovery proportion. Choosing among many analyses after seeing the results creates the same problem without a visible count.

Units in the target population have a meaningful chance of appearing in either the treated or the comparison group. This is also called common support. Without overlap, a comparison relies on extrapolation, and matching can leave treated units unmatched.

A p-value is the probability of a result at least as extreme as the one observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true. A result is statistically significant when the p-value is at or below a chosen threshold α, often 0.05. A result that is not significant does not show the effect is zero.

The difference-in-differences assumption that treated and comparison groups would have had the same average change in outcome without treatment. Pre-treatment trends can reveal an implausible comparison, but they cannot confirm the assumption after treatment.

The outcomes a unit would have under each treatment condition, written Y(1) with treatment and Y(0) without. Only one is observed for each unit, so causal effects compare group averages under assumptions that make the missing outcomes estimable.

The probability that a test rejects the null hypothesis when a specified true effect exists, given the design, sample size and significance level. Set the effect size to the smallest difference that would change the decision.

In a Bayesian analysis, the prior describes what is assumed about a parameter before seeing the data. The posterior combines the prior with the data through the likelihood, and a credible interval is a range of the posterior. In the marketing mix lessons, priors on channel effects can come from lift tests.

The probability that a unit receives treatment given its observed pre-treatment covariates. It is used to check overlap and to match, stratify or weight comparison groups. It differs from a response model’s predicted probability of an outcome, such as churn risk, and from uplift, which estimates how treatment changes the outcome.

Assigning treatment by a chance mechanism fixed before assignment, so that assignment is unrelated to the units’ potential outcomes. It supports estimating the effect of assignment among the enrolled units. Generalizing to a wider population requires random sampling or other assumptions.

The modeled relationship between spend on a channel and its outcome. Average return divides the channel’s modeled contribution by its total spend. Marginal return is the slope at the current spend, the additional outcome from a small increase.

Revenue divided by ad spend. Its meaning depends on the revenue counted. Apparent or platform-reported ROAS uses observed or credited revenue, including sales that would have occurred anyway. Incremental ROAS uses the revenue a causal comparison attributes to the spend. Average ROAS divides by total spend, and marginal ROAS is the return on the next dollar. The MMM calibration lesson calls incremental revenue per dollar of spend ROI.

A difference between the recorded number of units in each arm and the planned allocation, checked with a goodness-of-fit test. An SRM is a reason to trace assignment, logging and exclusions before interpreting the results.

Diminishing response at higher spend: beyond some point, each additional dollar adds less outcome. On an S-shaped curve, such as a Hill curve with exponent above 1, marginal return rises first, peaks and then declines. A marketing mix model can apply saturation before or after adstock.

Bias from how units enter the treated group or the observed data. Self-selection, such as frequent buyers joining a loyalty program, mixes the effect with preexisting differences. Selective observation, such as spending recorded only for customers who link receipts, can bias estimates even without a treatment comparison.

One unit’s treatment changes another unit’s outcome, such as advertising in one market reaching shoppers in a neighboring market. It is also called interference. Spillover can contaminate the control group. Designs either keep comparisons outside the exposure or measure exposure and estimate its effect.

The estimated standard deviation of an estimate across repeated samples, a measure of its precision. A t-statistic divides an estimate by its standard error. Standard errors must reflect the design, such as clustered assignment or reused matched controls.

Has two meanings in the guide. In market basket analysis, support is the share of baskets that contain a pair of items. In causal comparisons and models, support is where data exist: overlap means both groups appear at the covariate values of interest, and a model’s fit outside its training support relies on assumptions rather than data.

Survival is the share of a starting group still active at a given time. The hazard is the rate of leaving among those still active. With a constant hazard, the chance of staying another month does not depend on how long a customer has already stayed.

The difference in an outcome, such as conversion probability, under treatment versus control for customers with a given baseline profile. It is a conditional average treatment effect. Targeting by uplift contacts profiles whose expected benefit exceeds the contact cost, which differs from targeting by churn or purchase risk.
